evidence.E1: The decision is structural, not commentary. app.py:232-237 returns the response object with `background=BackgroundTask(dispatcher.dispatch, claimed)` — the sync part (verify, claim, persist, parse) is steps 1-5 in the endpoint body, and everything after the acknowledgement is a separate module (`dispatch.py`) driven by three callers: the request path, `recovery.py`'s `RecoverySweep`, and `cli.py`'s replay. The consequence of that choice is carried through consistently: at-least-once delivery is stated as the handler contract (handlers.py:1-30), the `RecoverySweep` exists specifically for the crash-after-202 window (recovery.py:1-11), and dispatch.py:102-114 leaves the row in `received` when the terminal write fails so the sweep re-drives it. The ordering is enforced by a test at the ASGI layer (test_receive.py:237), not merely asserted in prose.
evidence.E2: No secret literals in `src/`: config.py:166-183 resolves each sender's secret only via `env.get(variable)` from `secret_envs`, and a missing/empty variable is a startup abort (config.py:178-181, tests/unit/test_config.py:54 and :62). senders.example.toml:3-6 states secrets are never written to the file and only names env vars. Confirmed by running the service with the secrets supplied purely through the environment. `.gitignore` exists and the shipped example carries no real values; the only byte-strings in the tree that look like secrets are test fixtures (tests/conftest.py:20-22).
evidence.E3: Followed README.md:104-131 literally and it worked end to end with no other information: `cp senders.example.toml senders.toml`, `export WEBHOOK_SECRET_ACME=...` (plus the other three the example file names), `webhook-receiver serve --config senders.toml --db ./webhooks.db --port 8971` -> banner listing all three senders and `listening http://127.0.0.1:8971`. unanticipated_findings: README.md:127 documents a second way to run the service — `uvicorn webhook_receiver.app:create_app --factory --port 8000` — which cannot work. `create_app` (src/webhook_receiver/app.py:78) takes `config` as a required positional argument and there is no zero-argument factory that loads `senders.toml` from the environment. Reproduced verbatim: `cd /tmp/e2eF && uvicorn webhook_receiver.app:create_app --factory --port 8972` -> `ERROR:    Error loading ASGI app factory: create_app() missing 1 required positional argument: 'config'`. This matters more than a typo because the same README paragraph (app.py:137-139 repeats the claim in a code comment) treats the factory path as the supported way to run under a process manager, and app.py:140 logs `config.loaded` specifically 'because under --factory there is no banner' — so the code was written around a deployment mode that does not function.

Three prose blocks are truncated mid-sentence, in files a reader is directed to. src/webhook_receiver/recovery.py:11 ends `The sweep dies with the process. A crash-looping service recovers nothing; that` and then the docstring closes. senders.example.toml:33-34 ends `...which is why the deliveries table is` immediately before the `[senders.globex]` table header, so the reasoning for the globex sender's only replay defence is cut off. README.md:220-223 jumps from numbered step 3 to step 5 with a dangling fragment `breaks one of them needs to say so explicitly and argue for it.` and README.md:157 reads `- Full surface, including the CLI and the log vocabulary:` followed by nothing — a link that was never written. None of this affects behaviour, but the artefact ships documentation that stops mid-thought in four places.

The integration-level replay-window parameters use a hardcoded epoch that is a year off the test clock, so one of them does not test what it names. tests/integration/test_receive.py:29-30 build `timestamp_too_old` as `1754481600 - 3600` and `timestamp_too_new` as `1754481600 + 3600`, but 1754481600 is 2025-08-06T12:00Z while `FakeClock` starts at 2026-08-06T12:00Z (tests/conftest.py:29). Both stamps are therefore roughly one year in the *past*; the `timestamp_too_new` case exercises the stale branch, not the future-skew branch, and would still pass if the `abs()` at src/webhook_receiver/signature.py:166 were removed. Reproduce: change signature.py:166 to `if skew > self.replay_window_seconds:` — tests/integration/test_receive.py still passes all 7 params. (The unit test at tests/unit/test_signature.py:156 does cover future skew correctly and would catch it, so the property is not actually unprotected — but the integration parameter is mislabelled and contributes nothing.)

The recovery sweep sleeps before its first pass, so a restart recovers nothing for a full interval. src/webhook_receiver/recovery.py:86-88: `while True: await asyncio.sleep(self.interval_seconds)` then `sweep_once()`. After a crash, deliveries stranded in `received` — precisely the case recovery.py:8-9 says the sweep exists for — wait `sweep_interval_seconds` (default 60 s, senders.example.toml:10) on top of `stale_after_seconds` before anything looks at them, even though they were already provably stale at boot. Swapping the order (sweep, then sleep) would cost nothing, since `sweep_once` already no-ops on a fresh database (asserted by tests/integration/test_recovery.py:158). Low severity, but it is the one moment the sweep is most needed and the only one where it is guaranteed idle.

For a `stable_body` sender the dedup key is derived from the body alone, dropping the timestamp that the same request just proved was fresh. src/webhook_receiver/app.py:75 computes `sha256(sender.name + raw_body)`, while the `timestamped-hmac-sha256` scheme signs `f"{timestamp}.{body}"` — so two genuinely distinct events with byte-identical payloads sent minutes apart collapse into one delivery and the second is silently answered 200 with no handler call. The shipped example configures exactly this combination (senders.example.toml:51-59: `initech`, timestamped scheme, `stable_body = true`). The risk is called out honestly at senders.example.toml:45-50, and including the timestamp would break dedup across a sender's own retries, so this is a defensible trade rather than a bug — recording it because the hazard is a configuration choice an operator makes in a TOML file, and its consequence (dropped events, invisible to both ends) is the exact failure the service exists to prevent.
